narrative: Five tickets over four months, mostly onboarding and configuration questions handled within a week. The one snag - dashboard visibility restrictions not respecting access groups - was raised as a calm follow-up and resolved without recurrence. No complaints, no urgency language; a setup-phase account settling into steady use.

Eighteen months of consistently friendly, curiosity-driven tickets - export templates, API pagination, feature requests - all resolved quickly with zero complaints. The account is expanding (new Oslo office dashboard, a seat audit ahead of renewal) and volunteers unprompted positive feedback ('loving how much time the scheduled exports are saving us'). A model healthy relationship.

Heavy, high-urgency ticket volume across nearly a year - connector outages, permission reverts, corrupted exports, four separate issues logged on one day in September ('on top of the other three tickets today') - but every issue closes in one to two days with no repeat failures reported afterward. This reads as an intensively engaged power-user account hitting real operational friction, not a relationship pulling back; worth monitoring for reliability trends but no sign of lost patience.

Five low-stakes admin and how-to tickets spread across a year, all resolved without friction. Routine account maintenance (seat additions, a departure, a dashboard tiling question) with no complaints or recurring faults - unremarkable in the best sense.

In Storsund BI we had grouped subtotals that collapsed by default. Is there an equivalent here, or do I need to build that manually with a calculated field?

narrative: A recent-migration account working through feature-parity gaps against its old tool (Storsund BI), all raised as calm comparison questions rather than complaints. The one flag worth watching: the final ticket reveals a regional manager has been quietly rebuilding dashboard numbers by hand in Excel rather than trusting the export - the kind of unspoken workaround that can precede disengagement even though the ticket itself was resolved same-day.

Four spaced-out, low-severity tickets over four months - a billing discrepancy, a filename request, a 2FA reset, one user's stale dashboard cache. All routine, all resolved within days, no tone of frustration. Healthy, quiet account.

A rough second half of 2024 - silent connector failures, a three-week broken export ('this needs a real fix, not another we're looking into it'), then unreliable alerts prompting an explicit escalation demand ('I'd like this escalated properly... I need someone to look at our account as a whole, not ticket by ticket'). The arc then resolves: by March 2025 the customer confirms the connector fix held ('stable since the fixes went in, no failures') and the filter fix is holding too, and the rest of the year is calm feature questions and positive follow-ups. Textbook anger-to-resolution recovery, not an account at risk today.

Sanna Koskinen has logged eight distinct problems in six months across alerts, API, dashboards and connectors, each one explicitly tied back to the last ('this is the second alert issue we have had', 'we had rate limit issues in October and now token stability'). Resolution times are stretching (21 days for alerts wiped by a platform update, 10 days for a scheduler outage) and the tone has moved from polite to direct demands ('Scheduler down AGAIN... Escalate', 'I need this looked at properly'). An account accumulating unaddressed systemic reliability problems with an increasingly impatient single point of contact.

Three sparse, unrelated how-to and minor-bug tickets across almost a year, each resolved in a few days with no follow-up complaints. Low volume here reflects genuine quiet, not suppressed frustration - no recurring themes or unresolved threads.

Two contacts (Matti Lehtinen, Sigrid Larsson) reported a cluster of problems in mid-2024, including an API slowdown that sat unaddressed across two tickets ('I raised this with your chat support and was told to submit a ticket. Still waiting' ... 'Two open tickets now') before finally closing. A SQL connector dropping columns, reported 25 July, was logged as unresolved and never mentioned again - genuinely open at the end of the record. The final two tickets (October) are calm, routine fixes, suggesting the acute frustration passed, but the connector data-loss issue has no confirmed resolution in the text.
Five well-spaced, low-key tickets over eight months - export timing checks, formatting and comparison feature questions - all resolved without complaint. Textbook healthy low-touch account.
A single API scoping question, resolved in four days. Too little history to read a trend, but nothing here suggests any friction.

An openly enthusiastic account ('Team is very happy with the platform so far') that is visibly growing - nearly 20 seats now, a new product line - and a September return visit that patiently follows up on a months-old feature discussion rather than escalating ('still interested in the better export retention settings we discussed before'). Two feature requests remain unbuilt but are framed as nice-to-haves, not blockers; the closing ticket reports the delivered rolling-average alert 'has been working very well.'

Sparse, calm traffic across thirteen months with explicit acknowledgement of quiet periods ('Been a while since our last ticket, everything's been running smoothly'). A workaround for a formatting request was accepted without complaint ('the workaround you suggested has worked fine'). One pending feature request (alert history export) is a mild nice-to-have, not a sign of trouble.

A short but pointed history: the NetSuite connector auth error reported in August recurred in September, 'this time twice in one week,' with the customer explicitly asking whether something structural is causing the token to keep dropping. The batch ends on that unanswered question with no confirmation the root cause was found - a recurring integration fault the resolved flag doesn't reflect.

competitor_mentions.quote: We're evaluating a couple of alternatives for next year including Storsund BI, partly on the strength of their more granular permissions model, so a proper fix here would help make the comparison fair.

We're continuing our evaluation of Storsund BI as part of the broader tooling review, and reliability of connector auth is one of the things we're weighing directly against what we've experienced here.

narrative: Only three tickets in four months, but each is long, precise, and explicitly ties a specific admin-side fault (a permission role reverting, then an unannounced connector token revocation - 'the second admin-side surprise in a few months') to an active, named vendor evaluation against Storsund BI. This is the quiet pattern that matters more than volume: a meticulously documented account weighing whether to leave, with reliability of exactly the account-admin functions under active procurement comparison. Deserves direct outreach regardless of the fast individual ticket resolutions.

A consistently positive, growing account across eight months - unprompted praise ('exports have been noticeably faster since the last release'), a 12-seat Stockholm expansion, and a feature request (percentage alert thresholds) that shipped and drew genuine follow-up praise ('worked really well for us... very happy with how this turned out'). No friction anywhere in the record.

A widget-loading fault recurred once ('same symptom as the ticket from late November') before being fixed for good, alongside unrelated one-off formula and API rate-limit issues. No repeat complaints after the second widget fix, and no signs of frustration building. Routine account with occasional bugs, promptly handled.
A single data-sync discrepancy ticket, resolved in two days. Not enough history to read a trend, but the one interaction was calm and factual.

Three tickets in three months with resolution times drifting longer (8, 4, then 13 days), including a formula bug the customer had to nudge on themselves ('wanted to flag that it's been open a couple of weeks now, in case it's slipped through'). No anger or competitor talk, but the lengthening response times and self-initiated follow-up are worth watching.
